name: Clallam
world_status: statement found in an open source

new_statements.quote: 1. Stress assignment. The rules assigning stress to syllables are the fundamental determinants of whether the syllable will contain a vowel of predictable or unpredictable quality. As in Northern Straits and other Salishan languages stress assignment is generally morphologically conditioned--certain suffixes attract stress. In Klallam as in Saanich there is a tendency to penultimate stress other things being equal. I leave a fuller description of Klallam stress placement for a later study. It suffices here simply to say that primary stress is assigned to one of the vowels of the fully derived word.
new_statements.citation: Montler, Timothy. 1998. The major processes affecting Klallam vowels. Papers for the 33rd International Conference on Salish and Neighboring Languages, Seattle: University of Washington, pp. 366-373.
new_statements.locator: Section listing the processes, item '1. Stress assignment' (author's PDF p. 3 = 4th PDF page; within pp. 366-373 of the ICSNL 33 volume)

new_statements.rule_in_words: One primary stress per (fully derived) word; its position is determined morphologically -- roots and suffixes differ in whether they take/attract stress (Montler 2015 Sec. 31.1: weak stems shift the accented vowel rightward under suffixation, strong stems keep it, zero stems have no stressable vowel and a stressed suffix or inserted schwa carries stress; Sec. 40.1: suffixes like causative -istxw take stress from the root, whose vowel then reduces to schwa) -- with a default tendency toward the penultimate syllable when morphology does not decide. Unstressed full vowels reduce to schwa and unstressed schwa deletes, so stress is marked lexically with an acute in the orthography.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Nothing said about secondary stress in the 1998 paper ('primary stress is assigned to one of the vowels'); the 2015 grammar (Sec. 41.6) notes the particle ay'ngen carries its own stress without removing the host word's stress, otherwise one accent per stressable word.
new_statements.exceptions: Montler 2015 Sec. 40.1: seven stems keep their stress when causative -istxw is added; Sec. 31.1: no way to tell weak from strong t-stems by shape, 'most other stems are weak stems'; particles (u 'question', ya? 'past') never stressed.
new_statements.domain_note: Word level: 'primary stress is assigned to one of the vowels of the fully derived word' (1998); grammar: only 'stressable words' (verbs, nouns, adjectives, numbers, focus pronouns, intensifiers) bear an accent, short grammatical particles never do. Pitch and length not distinctive (Montler 2004).
new_statements.identity_note: All sources describe Klallam proper (clal1241; Elwha/Jamestown/Port Gamble speakers, Montler's fieldwork mainly Lower Elwha and Becher Bay). Montler explicitly compares with Saanich/Northern Straits (stra1244), which is a separate language already in the catalog.

sources.note: Process 1 'Stress assignment': stress assignment is generally morphologically conditioned (certain suffixes attract stress), with a tendency to penultimate stress other things being equal; primary stress assigned to one vowel of the fully derived word; unstressed i/u/a reduce to schwa, unstressed schwa deletes; stressed vowels longer (except stressed schwa). Fuller description of stress placement deferred to a later study.

sources.note: Pedagogical: stress is written with an acute on every stressable word (verbs, nouns, adjectives, numbers, focus pronouns, intensifiers); particles never stressed; stressed vowel louder and longer. Sec. 31.1: three stem types -- weak stems (accented vowel moves right when suffixes added, mist -> mesiteng), strong stems (accent stays), zero stems (no accented vowel, schwa inserted or stressed suffix takes stress); Sec. 40.1: causative -istxw 'usually takes the stress away from the root', root vowel then becomes schwa, seven stems keep their stress.
